title: Postcard and Orchard
premise: Marine biologist Wendell Iversen has spent a decade training the heart like any other muscle—contained, measurable, safe—hiding behind turtle counts and a career that once pulled them back from the edge. When their grandmother's will demands every heir attend the family orchard reunion or forfeit their inheritance, Wendell hires Marisol Vega, a struggling orchard-hand-turned-improv-artist, to pose as their partner for one weekend. But the fake romance curdles into something real by dessert, and as the festival unfolds, Wendell uncovers the truth of how the orchard was won: a land deal built on a buried injustice against Marisol's own family. By the final night, Wendell must choose between the grant-funded future that saved their life and the person who finally sees them—and between keeping an inheritance bought with someone else's loss, or burning it down for justice no court will deliver.
about_author: Wren Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former field researcher who traded tide charts for love stories set in places where the past refuses to stay buried. They write from a coastal cottage shared with two rescue dogs and an unreasonable number of houseplants.

chapters.title: Counting Turtles
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. On a research vessel, Wendell catalogs sea turtles and deflects a colleague's concern about their isolation, insisting the heart is trainable muscle. A letter arrives: Grandmother Iversen's will requires all heirs at the orchard reunion—or forfeiture. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness cracking under obligation.

chapters.title: The Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Flashback to the childhood summers at Iversen Orchard and the year Wendell nearly drowned—the career that 'saved everything' was born there. The lawyer's letter reveals a strange clause: heirs must arrive 'with their lives in order.' Wendell panics; they have no partner to show. Beat: dread dressed as practicality.

chapters.title: A Woman at the Fish Market
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Buying supplies, Wendell watches Marisol Vega talk a vendor down from a price war with pure charm and improvisation. Something about her ease aches. Wendell blurts out an absurd offer before thinking. Beat: reckless hope disguised as logistics.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Over bad coffee, Wendell and Marisol negotiate: paid weekend, scripted backstory, zero feelings. Marisol needs rent money and a stage; Wendell needs a shield. They shake on it. Both privately note the handshake lasted too long. Beat: contract signed, chemistry unaccounted for.

chapters.title: The Long Drive North
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Road trip cram session—names, dates, how they met (a lie about a farmers market). Marisol catches Wendell flinching at a bridge and files it away without comment. Beat: intimacy beginning through small, unscripted observations.

chapters.title: Arrival at Iversen Orchard
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The orchard in late bloom; cousins sizing up the couple like appraisers. Aunt Dorothea, executor of the will, greets them with a smile that doesn't reach her eyes. Marisol performs flawlessly. Beat: performance versus belonging.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. At the welcome dinner, Marisol improvises a story about Wendell that is so tender it lands too true. Wendell goes quiet, eyes bright. Under the table, hands almost touch. Beat: the fake date feels real by dessert—exactly as promised.

chapters.title: Old Ghosts in the Rows
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Unable to sleep, Wendell walks the orchard and finds Marisol staring at a boundary stone, pale. She deflects. Wendell notices the name carved there isn't an Iversen. Beat: first crack in both their secrets.

chapters.title: Rehearsed and Unrehearsed
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Festival prep montage: cider pressing, lantern hanging. A cousin forces them into a couples' game; Marisol answers questions about Wendell with truths she couldn't possibly know yet. Wendell stares. Beat: falling in public while pretending not to.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Hunting for spare linens, Wendell finds Grandmother's old ledgers in the attic—a 1998 payment to 'V. Vega' marked 'settled, say nothing.' Wendell pockets the page, heart hammering. Beat: inheritance revealed as something darker than legacy.

chapters.title: The Storm Delay
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A storm strands everyone indoors; power fails. Candlelight, one blanket, confessions traded like currency—Wendell admits the drowning, the years of numbness. Marisol says 'I know what water takes' and stops herself. Beat: closeness at maximum, secrets straining.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Morning after the storm, a near-kiss interrupted by Aunt Dorothea announcing the will's reading schedule. Wendell retreats into turtle statistics; Marisol's face closes like a door. Beat: retreat after vulnerability—the trained heart reasserting itself.

chapters.title: Vega
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts her mother by phone: yes, this is THAT orchard, the one that took their farm in '98. Her mother begs her to leave. Marisol looks at sleeping Wendell and stays. Beat: loyalty split between blood and something new.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Will
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Dorothea reads the will aloud; the 'lives in order' clause is revealed as a test of character, and the orchard passes to whichever heir Dorothea judges worthy. Cousins begin performing virtue. Wendell realizes the whole weekend is an audition. Beat: stakes sharpened.

chapters.title: Boundary Stone
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol tells Wendell the truth: the orchard sits on land her grandfather lost to a predatory loan orchestrated by the Iversens; the ledger payment was hush money. Wendell's inheritance is stolen ground. Beat: collision of love and justice.

chapters.title: Muscle Memory
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell spirals—confronting Dorothea means losing everything, including the career funded by family money. They coldly suggest Marisol take the hush fund and walk away. Marisol, hurt, agrees to leave after the festival. Beat: the price of survival made explicit; self-sabotage.

chapters.title: Festival Eve
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Packing alone, Marisol finds Wendell's old journal left in the guest room—pages proving Wendell traced the Vega debt months ago and came here intending to make it right, then lost their nerve. Beat: evidence that love and courage were always entangled.

chapters.title: The Lantern Festival
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The whole town gathers; Dorothea prepares to announce her chosen heir. Wendell searches the crowd for Marisol and doesn't find her. Onstage, Dorothea begins her speech. Beat: held breath, everything converging.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Climax. Wendell interrupts the announcement, reads the 1998 ledger entry aloud, and publicly renounces their claim, demanding the orchard be returned or sold to the Vegas at its true history's price. Dorothea threatens ruin; Wendell chooses the person over the prize. Beat: the trained heart finally breaking open on purpose.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Fallout: furious relatives, a stunned Dorothea who quietly admits she engineered the clause hoping someone would do exactly this. Marisol finds Wendell at the boundary stone. No grand speech—just a real first kiss. Beat: release.

chapters.title: Grafting Season
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Weeks later: legal slow wheels turn, but the Vegas hold the deed's promise; Wendell takes a coastal research post within driving distance. They plant a new tree together where the stone stands. Beat: rebuilding on honest ground.

chapters.title: Postcard
chapters.summary: Epilogue, alternating letters/postcards between chapters of their new life. Final image: a postcard of the orchard in bloom, addressed to Grandmother's memory—'We kept it. We fixed it. We stayed.' Beat: quiet, earned resolution.
